dataAnalysis.title: Race Analysis
dataAnalysis.content:
The rise of the Republican Party in the Lone Star State is a fascinating tale of how one party consistently cut off its nose to spite its face. Texas always had a small Republican Party in the Panhandle, in the German counties around San Antonio, and later in the growing suburbs of Dallas and Houston. But the two-party system mostly played out among Democrats. That party was divided between conservative Tory Democrats, who sought to deny Franklin Roosevelt Texas’s electoral votes in 1944 and who supported President Eisenhower in the 1950s, and the liberal Democrats.

When LBJ was elected vice president, a conservative appointee replaced him. In the ensuing special election, liberal Democrats either stayed home or cast a protest vote for Republican John Tower, whom they figured they could easily defeat later. The same dynamic played out in 1966, allowing Tower’s re-election. By 1972 Tory Democrats were defecting to the Republican Party, while the Republicans’ native base in the suburbs continued to grow.

Today the Republicans have controlled the governorship for more than 30 straight years and both Senate seats for 33. Democrats haven’t won a statewide race since 1994. The long-promised Democratic revival fueled by immigration hasn’t arrived; if anything, Hispanic voters moved toward Donald Trump in 2024, when he carried the state by 14 points. But Republicans may be about to learn the lesson Democrats learned in 1961. In May, GOP voters threw out four-term Sen. John Cornyn in favor of Attorney General Ken Paxton, who campaigned with Trump’s endorsement. To say Paxton brings considerable baggage is an understatement; his 2023 impeachment by the Republican state House alone would be a red flag in most environments. Democrats nominated state Rep. James Talarico, a Presbyterian seminarian who beat Rep. Jasmine Crockett in March and who is running as the sort of Democrat who can win crossover voters. Polls show Talarico with a small but consistent lead, usually in the high 40s. Texas has broken Democratic hearts before, and undecided voters here probably lean Republican. But this is a real race, and if Paxton loses, Republicans will have only themselves to blame.
